patient.chief_complaint: Continuous generalized seizure for 20 minutes, known epilepsy, missed antiepileptic medications for 3 days
patient.hpi: A 36-year-old White male software engineer with a 10-year history of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) was brought to the emergency department by his girlfriend via EMS after a continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His girlfriend reports he began convulsing while watching television at approximately 9:45 PM. He initially had bilateral arm jerking (myoclonic) that rapidly evolved into a full generalized tonic-clonic seizure and continued without stopping. EMS was called 5 minutes after onset. He arrived continuously convulsing — total seizure duration at ED arrival was 22 minutes. EMS administered IV lorazepam 4 mg enroute without effect. He has a longstanding diagnosis of JME confirmed by video-EEG 8 years ago, showing 3-4 Hz generalized polyspike-wave discharges with prominent morning myoclonic jerks. He was well-controlled on valproate 1500 mg/day for 6 years until 2 years ago when he was switched to levetiracetam 1500 mg BID due to weight gain. He has been stable with levetiracetam. His girlfriend reports he ran out of levetiracetam 3 days ago and was trying to 'get by' until his next prescription was refilled. He works long hours and had been sleep-deprived for the past week (known JME trigger). No alcohol or drug use. No fever. No recent illness. He has no medication allergies. Family history: sister has absence epilepsy. Social history: non-smoker, occasional beer on weekends (none this week per girlfriend), no illicit drugs. He is a software engineer currently working remotely on a deadline project.

Clinical management: reload levetiracetam IV immediately, educate about medication adherence and JME triggers (sleep deprivation). Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions.description: Phenytoin and fosphenytoin are CONTRAINDICATED in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) and other idiopathic generalized epilepsies. Phenytoin is a sodium channel blocker that preferentially blocks fast-spiking neurons but does NOT suppress T-type calcium channel-mediated absence/myoclonic activity. In JME patients, phenytoin can paradoxically WORSEN myoclonus and absence seizures by disinhibiting thalamocortical circuits. Multiple case series demonstrate clinical deterioration with phenytoin in JME. This is a well-established clinical teaching point.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: NEVER use phenytoin or fosphenytoin in JME or any idiopathic generalized epilepsy. Use levetiracetam (first-line), valproate (effective but teratogenic), lamotrigine (second-line), or clonazepam for JME. For JME SE: IV lorazepam + IV levetiracetam loading. If JME SE refractory: IV valproate is second-line.

output.summary: Phenytoin/fosphenytoin CONTRAINDICATED in JME — worsens myoclonus and absence. IV levetiracetam is the correct AED. Valproate is effective for JME but has teratogenicity concerns. Lamotrigine is third-line for JME.

results.title: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: long-term outcomes and management
results.key_finding: JME is a lifelong epilepsy requiring maintenance AED therapy. Key triggers for breakthrough seizures and SE: sleep deprivation, alcohol, medication non-adherence (strongest predictor). Levetiracetam and valproate are most effective for JME. Phenytoin/carbamazepine/vigabatrin worsen JME. Medication adherence education and automated refill programs reduce breakthrough SE risk by 70%. Most JME patients require lifelong treatment.

output.summary: JME management: lifelong medication adherence is critical. Major triggers: sleep deprivation, alcohol, missed medications. Levetiracetam first-line; phenytoin contraindicated. Automated refill programs prevent medication lapses. Educate patient about SE risk with missed doses.

critical_actions: IV lorazepam immediately for convulsive SE
IV levetiracetam 2000 mg loading dose — restore therapeutic level
Phenytoin/fosphenytoin ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in JME — worsens myoclonus and absence
Levetiracetam level confirms non-adherence — address medication adherence at discharge
Normal CT confirms no structural precipitant — JME is idiopathic generalized epilepsy
contraindicated_actions: Phenytoin or fosphenytoin for JME SE — contraindicated in idiopathic generalized epilepsy, worsens myoclonus and absence seizures
Carbamazepine for long-term JME management — worsens absence and myoclonic components
Discharging without levetiracetam refill — prescription lapse was the direct cause; must provide refill before discharge
key_reasoning_points: JME + undetectable AED level = medication non-adherence is the precipitant — the most common cause of SE in patients with known epilepsy

Phenytoin/fosphenytoin CONTRAINDICATED in JME — blocks fast Na+ channels in cortical neurons but does not suppress the thalamocortical T-type calcium channel circuits mediating JME; can paradoxically worsen myoclonus
Levetiracetam IV loading is the correct approach: 2000 mg IV bolus restores therapeutic levels rapidly, safe and effective
JME triggers are critical counseling points: sleep deprivation, alcohol, medication non-adherence — all three were present in this case
Post-ictal leukocytosis is a stress response, not infection — do not initiate empiric antibiotics based on WBC elevation alone in a post-ictal patient with clear precipitant
Serial troponin trending down confirms neurogenic cardiac stress, not NSTEMI — differentiation from Type 2 MI requires trending

metadata.teaching_points: JME non-adherence causing SE; phenytoin CONTRAINDICATED in JME; levetiracetam IV loading; post-ictal leukocytosis vs infection; neurogenic troponin elevation
metadata.pitfalls: Using phenytoin for JME SE; missing medication non-adherence as precipitant; treating post-ictal leukocytosis as infection; discharging without medication refill
metadata.clinical_pearl: JME + SE: IV lorazepam + IV levetiracetam. Phenytoin CONTRAINDICATED — worsens JME. Undetectable levetiracetam = non-adherence = direct cause. Discharge with prescription + trigger education.
